task.goal: Teach twelve teenagers to distinguish map distance from travel time when planning a walking route.
hard_constraints: Use printed maps, rulers and a classroom clock; no phones or actual street crossing during the lesson.
Do not imply that a straight-line distance is a safe or accessible route.
In 35 minutes, check each learner's ability to explain scale, route choice and uncertainty.
task.available_resources: Two printed neighborhood maps with scales, pencils and example walking speeds.
task.expected_result: An accessible lesson with a short individual check.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Compare routes: shorter distance can take longer
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners compare two mapped walking routes between the same endpoints, separating route length from travel time. A longer route can take less time under explicitly stated speed and delay assumptions. The comparison makes the distinction concrete without treating straight-line distance as a usable walking route.

Use the two printed maps at two tables of six, with rulers, pencils, example walking speeds and the classroom clock. Assume the maps show legible scales and connected paths. If accessibility or crossing information is absent, describe both routes as planning possibilities requiring verification. Any invented delay is a hypothetical teaching assumption, not a neighborhood fact.

Minutes 0–5: demonstrate reading the scale and converting a ruler measurement into ground distance. Trace a route along mapped paths, measuring and adding its segments. Explain that estimated time equals route distance divided by walking speed, plus assumed delays.

Minutes 5–15: each table measures two routes; rotate measuring, tracing and explaining so all six participate. Give one route a hypothetical waiting delay and calculate both estimates using a supplied speed. Minutes 15–20: compare route choices, then change the speed or delay and reconsider. Minutes 20–23: rehearse explanations and discuss missing information, including surface, steps and crossing arrangements.

Minutes 23–35: conduct twelve individual one-minute checks beside a map. Each learner interprets its scale, explains a route choice using distance and time, and names an uncertainty that could change the estimate or choice. Permit pointing, spoken explanations and an adult reading labels aloud. Larger shared views and verbal descriptions support access, although very small print may remain a limitation.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During the individual check, first ask which route is shorter, then which would take less time under the stated assumptions. Compare the explanation with the simple distance-only rule, 'choose the shorter route.' Change one delay and ask whether the choice changes. The mechanism has not worked for a learner who still equates shorter distance with less time, cannot interpret the scale, or treats an estimate as guaranteed. Record the three criteria with pencil on an unused map margin; distinguish arithmetic mistakes from conceptual confusion.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Run a tabletop journey against the classroom clock
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners observe elapsed time accumulating separately from mapped distance. A tabletop journey pauses while the clock continues, providing a visible example of why a ruler alone cannot predict arrival time.

Arrange two groups of six around the two maps. Use rulers, pencils, example walking speeds and the classroom clock. Select a short route along connected mapped paths on each map. No learner walks outside; a pointing finger represents progress. Map connections do not establish safe crossings or accessibility, which require further information.

Minutes 0–6: demonstrate the scale and measure a route in segments. Calculate its moving-time estimate using one supplied walking speed. Explain the simulation convention: for example, one classroom second represents one journey minute. This compressed clock is a model, not a measurement of real walking performance.

Minutes 6–14: run the journeys together. Learners rotate tracing, clock-watching, calculating and explaining. At announced times, advance the finger to the corresponding segment boundary. Introduce a clearly hypothetical stop, holding position while time passes. Pause afterward to compare unchanged route distance with increased elapsed time.

Minutes 14–20: repeat a short section with another supplied speed. Ask which quantities changed and which stayed fixed. Minutes 20–23: each group proposes a route choice and identifies information needed before recommending it, such as steps, surface or crossing conditions.

Minutes 23–35: give each learner a one-minute oral check using a map: interpret a scale measurement, explain a route choice under a speed and delay assumption, and name an uncertainty. Accept pointing and verbal arithmetic; read labels aloud when helpful. The approach needs a readable clock and teacher coordination. Compressed timing may confuse some learners, so keep real seconds and represented journey minutes explicitly labeled in speech.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before the simulation, ask learners to predict whether a stop changes distance, travel time, both or neither; collect answers by a simultaneous finger signal. Repeat with a different hypothetical stop afterward. The simple comparator is the original moving-time estimate without stops. During individual checks, ask why that estimate could understate arrival time. Failure to distinguish elapsed time from distance, or confusion between classroom seconds and journey minutes, is evidence that the simulation needs simplification rather than another timed round.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Plan backward from an arrival deadline
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners work backward from a required arrival time, treating travel time as a constraint rather than choosing a route from length alone. Comparing optimistic and slower estimates reveals how uncertainty affects departure time and route choice.

Use two groups of six sharing the printed maps, rulers, pencils, supplied walking speeds and classroom clock. Choose endpoints connected by mapped paths. Assume the scale is readable; do not infer safe crossings or accessibility from a printed connection. If the map lacks relevant details, make route recommendations conditional on checking them.

Minutes 0–6: model measuring a path segment, applying the map scale and adding segments. Explain distance divided by speed, with consistent units. Use the classroom clock to set a hypothetical arrival deadline.

Minutes 6–16: each table measures two possible routes. Learners take turns measuring and explaining. Calculate travel times using two supplied example speeds; if only one is supplied, add a clearly hypothetical delay scenario. Work backward from the deadline to find departure times. Explain that the resulting range covers the stated scenarios and is not a guaranteed bound.

Minutes 16–23: groups choose a route and departure time, explaining their assumptions. Change one condition, such as an additional five-minute delay, and ask them to revise the plan. A longer route should be preferred only when stated evidence or hypothetical conditions justify it; length alone establishes neither safety nor accessibility.

Minutes 23–35: twelve individual one-minute checks. Each learner explains what a ruler measurement means at the map scale, chooses between the measured routes with a reason, and identifies one uncertainty plus its possible effect on departure time. Learners may point, answer orally and use the group's existing calculations. Read map labels aloud as needed. Backward clock arithmetic adds cognitive demand, so use whole-minute examples and assess conceptual explanations separately from subtraction accuracy.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use 'leave at the deadline minus the fastest calculated walking time' as the simple comparator. In each individual check, introduce a hypothetical delay and ask whether that departure still meets the deadline and what should change. A successful explanation connects scale to distance, distance and assumptions to time, and uncertainty to an earlier departure or conditional route choice. If learners merely add an unexplained buffer or claim guaranteed arrival, the backward-planning activity has not established the intended distinction.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Repair a fictional planner’s mistakes
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners diagnose and repair a flawed route explanation. Identifying the exact step where a planner confuses map measurement, ground distance and travel time can reveal distinctions that copying a correct calculation may conceal. The outcome depends on learners explaining their repairs, rather than merely spotting an obviously wrong answer.

Use the two printed maps at tables of six, with rulers, pencils, example walking speeds and the classroom clock. The teacher presents short fictional statements orally; no additional handouts are needed. Assume the scales and some connected paths are legible. Provide correct arithmetic orally when necessary so calculation difficulty does not block conceptual participation.

Minutes 0–6: model measuring a route along mapped paths, converting its length using the scale, and estimating moving time from distance and speed. State that straight-line separation does not establish a usable route, and mapped connections do not establish safety or accessibility.

Minutes 6–15: present three fictional errors: 'These ruler centimetres are the actual walking distance'; 'This route is shorter, so it must always take less time'; and 'The map shows a path, so everyone can use it.' Each group locates the unsupported step and repairs the statement. For each error, two different learners explain a repair before open discussion, giving all twelve a speaking turn.

Minutes 15–23: groups build a corrected recommendation for one mapped route, explicitly separating measured distance, estimated time and information still needed. Discuss surfaces, steps, crossing arrangements and differences in walking speed without inventing neighborhood facts.

Minutes 23–35: conduct twelve individual one-minute checks beside a map. Each learner interprets a ruler measurement using the scale, repairs a route recommendation and names an uncertainty that could affect it. Accept oral answers, pointing and teacher-read labels. Small print remains a possible access limitation.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use a new fictional recommendation during each individual check, including a correct statement so learners cannot succeed by rejecting everything. Compare a bare accept/reject response with an explanation and repair. Ask what one ruler centimetre represents, whether the recommendation follows from the stated assumptions, and what missing fact could change it. Record scale, route-choice reasoning and uncertainty separately in a map margin. The mechanism is unsupported for a learner who recognizes familiar wording but cannot repair a new example or wrongly rejects a valid conditional estimate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Audit what the map can and cannot tell you
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners classify planning questions by the evidence needed to answer them. Separating what can be measured from what requires assumptions or further information teaches why a map distance alone cannot determine travel time or justify a route recommendation. The key change is deciding which conclusions the available evidence supports.

Use two groups of six sharing the maps, rulers, pencils, example walking speeds and classroom clock. Questions are delivered orally, with three response labels: 'map measurement,' 'estimate using assumptions,' and 'needs more information.' No cards or extra copies are required. Assume readable scales and identifiable mapped paths; the teacher reads labels and describes features when helpful.

Minutes 0–6: demonstrate interpreting scale and adding the lengths of a route's segments. Explain distance divided by speed in consistent units. A straight line may describe separation but does not establish a walking route.

Minutes 6–14: give six questions, allowing each learner at each table to lead one response: What ground distance does this ruler length represent? How long is this traced route? How long might it take at the supplied speed? What if there is an assumed stop? Does this path have steps? Is this crossing suitable for this walker? Learners identify the evidence needed and explain their classification. Accept overlap when justified: measuring route distance also depends on interpreting the map correctly.

Minutes 14–23: each table measures one route and prepares a conditional recommendation: distance, estimated time under named assumptions, and one unresolved fact that matters to choosing it. Teacher-supplied hypothetical facts may illustrate how a recommendation changes; label them explicitly as hypothetical.

Minutes 23–35: twelve individual one-minute checks ask each learner to interpret scale, justify a route choice with the available evidence, and identify an uncertainty and its possible effect. Oral answers and pointing are accepted. Classification labels support explanation but can become rote; require reasons rather than label recall.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use 'the map alone answers every planning question' as the simple comparator. In each individual check, ask one measurable question and one question the map cannot settle. Then supply a hypothetical speed or access detail and ask which conclusion it changes. Success requires an appropriate scale interpretation, a conditional route choice and a specific remaining uncertainty. A learner who says 'we cannot know anything' has also missed the distinction: ask them to identify a distance the map does support. This checks whether the activity builds calibrated judgment rather than blanket confidence or doubt.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Measure an indoor journey to discover what distance leaves out
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners observe real movement over a fixed indoor distance and measure its duration separately. The distance stays constant while observed times can vary; this makes walking speed an empirical link between distance and time. Measuring a person’s movement, rather than simulating a journey, also exposes timing uncertainty.

Prerequisites: a clear, accessible classroom strip approximately four metres long, permission for voluntary indoor movement, and a classroom clock displaying seconds. If these conditions are unavailable, this alternative is unsuitable. Use rulers to measure the strip and pencils placed safely on adjacent desks to identify its endpoints. Nobody must walk: timing, observing endpoints and explaining are equally useful roles. Do not ask anyone to hurry or compare learners’ performance.

Minutes 0–5: measure the strip together. Ask whether knowing its length determines how many seconds a journey will take. Demonstrate timing from starting movement to reaching the endpoint.

Minutes 5–11: a willing learner or teacher traverses it twice at comfortable, optionally different paces. Others read the clock and report elapsed seconds. Discuss why the distance remained fixed and why times might differ. Equal recorded times are possible; coarse clock readings and the short strip limit what the observations establish. Do not extrapolate these measurements into reliable outdoor walking speeds.

Minutes 11–17: split into two groups of six around the maps. Demonstrate scale conversion, then have learners measure connected route segments. Use the supplied example walking speeds to estimate time, keeping distance and time units explicit.

Minutes 17–23: each group explains a conditional route choice and identifies missing information about surfaces, steps or crossings. Straight-line separation establishes neither a walking route nor its safety or accessibility.

Minutes 23–35: give each learner a one-minute individual check beside a map. Accept spoken explanations, pointing and teacher-read labels; supply arithmetic results when needed to assess understanding separately from calculation.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Record three judgments per learner in a map margin: explains scale, justifies route choice using a time assumption, and names uncertainty with its possible effect. Against the simple rule ‘a measured distance determines one travel time,’ ask whether the same mapped route could take different times and why. Then ask what remains unchanged if walking speed changes. Failure to preserve distance while revising time, or treating the short indoor timing as a guaranteed outdoor prediction, falsifies the intended learning for that learner. These are proposed checks; no outcomes have been observed.

EXPAND.title: Build a units gate between distance and time
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: teach learners to check what a number measures before using it. A ruler and map scale produce distance; a walking speed is an additional input needed to estimate time. This targets the mistaken conversion from map length directly to minutes.

Preparation: the teacher selects a connected mapped route, checks its scale conversion and chooses a supplied walking speed with manageable arithmetic. Use the two maps at tables of six, rulers, pencils and the classroom clock. No additional printed materials are needed.

Minutes 0–6: demonstrate a three-stage calculation, writing in a map margin: centimetres on map → metres along route → estimated minutes. Explain each conversion aloud. Measure along mapped segments; a straight line between endpoints does not establish a usable, safe or accessible route.

Minutes 6–15: learners rotate through measuring, converting and explaining. Before accepting any answer, a peer asks, 'What is the unit, and what information allowed that conversion?' Give occasional incomplete prompts, such as route distance without speed. The appropriate answer is that distance is known but time cannot yet be estimated from the supplied information.

Minutes 15–23: apply the sequence to a second route. Learners explain a conditional route choice and identify missing information about delays, surfaces or accessibility. Supply a speed when requested so work continues after identifying the information gap.

Minutes 23–35: each learner receives a one-minute oral check covering scale, route choice using distance and time, and one uncertainty. Allow pointing, read labels aloud and provide arithmetic results when computation would obscure understanding.

The prerequisite is a readable map and scale. Unit labels can prevent category mistakes but cannot establish whether an assumed speed or route is realistic.
EXPAND.experiment: The teacher owns one 35-minute trial. Before teaching, collect simultaneous predictions about whether a scale alone determines walking minutes. At exit, use a different measurement and a missing-speed prompt. Compare with the strongest relevant prior approach, measuring and comparing two routes: look for better explanations of why speed is necessary, while recording time spent policing units. Stop the units routine if it consumes the practice period or learners merely recite labels without explaining the conversion. No improvement is established unless individual explanations improve without weakening route-choice and uncertainty answers.

EXPAND.title: Repair a plausible but faulty route recommendation
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: learners diagnose and repair someone else's reasoning. Explaining why a convincing recommendation fails can expose misconceptions that remain hidden when learners follow a correct worked example.

Preparation: the teacher selects connected paths on each printed map and checks one route measurement. In a map margin, write a short fictional recommendation containing three separable mistakes: misuse of scale, treating the shortest measured route as automatically fastest, and presenting arrival time as certain. Use only maps, rulers, pencils, supplied walking speeds and the classroom clock. The fictional claims are teaching examples, not neighborhood facts.

Minutes 0–5: model one correct scale conversion and distinguish route distance from estimated travel time. Explain that mapped connections do not verify crossing safety or accessibility; straight-line distance is not a walking recommendation.

Minutes 5–15: two groups of six audit the recommendation. Rotate responsibility for checking measurements, checking the time claim and checking certainty. Each learner must identify one claim and explain what evidence would support or contradict it. Read the recommendation aloud, and allow pointing instead of written annotation.

Minutes 15–23: groups repair the advice. Require a scale-based distance, a time estimate conditional on a supplied speed, and a route choice conditional on missing access or crossing information. If measurements disagree, the teacher provides the checked distance so discussion can proceed.

Minutes 23–35: twelve individual one-minute checks use a fresh short recommendation spoken by the teacher. Each learner interprets scale, repairs a route-choice justification and explains one uncertainty and its effect. Accept arithmetic support.

This approach assumes learners can follow a short argument. Keep errors few and finish with a correct explanation so the faulty claims do not become the most memorable lesson.
EXPAND.experiment: The teacher runs one lesson and records three exit criteria in a map margin. Compare with the prior correct worked-example and route-comparison approach using an unfamiliar recommendation: can learners explain the error and give sound advice themselves? Also record whether learners repeat the planted false claims or spend excessive time searching for tricks. Stop introducing faulty examples if misconceptions persist after correction; use the remaining practice time for an explicit correct model. The approach offers no gain if error spotting improves but independent scale, route-choice or uncertainty explanations do not.

EXPAND.title: Teach when a route estimate is ready—and when to ask
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: learners practice deciding whether the available information supports an estimate, a conditional plan or a request for verification. This directly teaches the boundary between useful planning and unjustified confidence.

Preparation: inspect the two maps and select connected candidate routes. Prepare spoken scenarios using the maps, supplied example speeds, rulers, pencils and classroom clock. Never describe an unverified crossing or path as safe or accessible.

Minutes 0–6: demonstrate scale and measure a route along its segments. Explain distance divided by speed as a moving-time estimate. Separate permission to calculate from evidence needed to recommend a route for someone's access needs.

Minutes 6–16: at two tables of six, discuss a close pair. In the first case, a route distance and example speed support a provisional moving-time estimate; crossing arrangements remain unverified, so using the route remains conditional. In the second, the same traveler must avoid steps and the map does not show whether steps exist. Learners can still report distance and conditional time, but should withhold an accessibility recommendation and ask a responsible adult or route authority to verify it. No outside contact occurs during the lesson.

Minutes 16–23: introduce an unfamiliar case involving an uncertain surface or walking speed. Learners identify what can be answered now, what cannot, and the specific information needed. Rotate speakers; read labels and questions aloud.

Minutes 23–35: each learner has one minute beside a map to explain scale, make a conditional route choice and address uncertainty. Present a concise close pair plus one unfamiliar variation, accepting brief spoken or pointed answers.

The decision rule is to continue useful calculations while withholding claims unsupported by the map. Its limit is that classroom reasoning cannot verify real-world route conditions.
EXPAND.experiment: The teacher owns one trial. Compare with the prior route-comparison lesson's general request to 'name an uncertainty.' Score whether each learner takes the appropriate action in both close cases and transfers it to the unfamiliar case, alongside scale and route-choice explanations. Track unnecessary refusal to estimate as the shifted cost. Stop adding scenarios if learners begin treating every missing detail as a reason to abandon planning; restate what can still be calculated. There is no improvement if learners merely mention more hazards without making better conditional decisions.

EXPAND.title: Reconstruct the missing question from a map answer
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: work backward from a claimed answer to the question and inputs it could legitimately answer. Learners discover that a distance answer and an arrival-time answer require different evidence. Reducing initial arithmetic lets them focus on the meaning of the result.

Preparation: the teacher checks a connected route on each map and writes its measured ground distance in a margin. Select a supplied walking speed and calculate the corresponding moving time. Use rulers, pencils and the classroom clock; the teacher must verify these calculations before presenting them.

Minutes 0–6: show the distance result and ask what question it answers. Demonstrate how the scale supports it. Explain why it does not, by itself, answer 'How long will the walk take?'

Minutes 6–15: two groups of six receive spoken answer fragments: a route distance, a moving-time estimate and a claimed arrival clock time. Learners reconstruct the necessary inputs for each: scale and path measurement; distance and assumed speed; then departure time and assumptions about delays. Rotate explanations so every learner contributes. Use the classroom clock to make departure and arrival meanings concrete without introducing a deadline-planning task.

Minutes 15–23: reveal a second mapped route. Learners explain what further evidence would justify choosing it. They may compare provided results without independently repeating every calculation. All route recommendations remain conditional on crossing and accessibility checks; straight-line distance establishes no usable walking route.

Minutes 23–35: conduct twelve one-minute checks. Each learner explains a scale conversion, selects a route under stated time assumptions and identifies an uncertainty that could alter the recommendation. Read labels aloud, allow pointing and supply calculation results when needed.

This approach requires carefully checked teacher examples. It reduces computation demands, but learners still need to demonstrate one scale interpretation individually; accepting supplied numbers alone would leave the goal unchecked.
EXPAND.experiment: The teacher runs one bounded lesson. Compare with the prior deadline approach, which adds backward clock arithmetic, and the route-comparison approach, which requires more group measurement. Use a fresh claim such as 'This route takes twelve minutes' and ask each learner what must be known to support it. Record the three goal criteria and dependence on teacher-provided answers. Stop supplying answer fragments during practice if learners accept them without examining their basis; require a ruler-and-scale demonstration. The approach has no advantage if reduced arithmetic produces weaker independent scale understanding or unsupported trust in estimates.

EXPAND.title: Compare routes with a measurement recovery rule
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: “Compare routes: shorter distance can take longer.” Preserve its primary mechanism: compare two mapped routes between the same endpoints using route distance, walking speed and hypothetical delays. Change the working procedure so a mistaken scale conversion cannot silently determine the entire comparison.

The teacher owns preparation and recovery. Use the two printed maps, rulers, pencils, supplied example speeds and classroom clock. Before the lesson, check that each map has a readable scale and two traceable candidate paths; independently measure their approximate lengths. Mapped connections do not establish safe crossings or accessibility. A straight line between endpoints is not a walking recommendation.

Minutes 0–6: model scale conversion, segmented route measurement and time = distance ÷ speed + assumed delays, using consistent units. Minutes 6–15: two tables of six measure two routes. Each learner measures or explains a segment. Before calculating times, a second learner checks the scale conversion and segment total. If the two results would reverse the distance ranking, the teacher checks the disputed segment immediately. Limit recovery to two minutes, then supply the teacher-checked distance and continue; learners must still explain its scale basis. This replaces prolonged measurement disputes rather than extending the lesson.

Minutes 15–21: compare times, using an explicitly hypothetical delay large enough to make the longer route faster under the supplied speed. Change that delay and reconsider the choice. Minutes 21–23: rehearse conditional recommendations and identify missing information about surfaces, steps and crossings.

Minutes 23–35: twelve individual one-minute checks. Each learner explains a scale conversion, chooses between the routes using distance and time, and names an uncertainty with its possible effect. Allow pointing, oral responses, label reading and supplied arithmetic results. Record these three criteria in a map margin.

If only one usable mapped path exists, compare two hypothetical journeys along it with different speeds or delays; ask learners to explain why an alternative route cannot yet be recommended. If neither scale is legible even with teacher support, the scale outcome cannot honestly be completed with these materials. Accessibility support is limited by the two shared maps and their print quality.
EXPAND.experiment: The teacher runs one 35-minute trial. Inspect whether independent checks catch disagreements before they affect route choices, whether recovery stays within two minutes, and whether every learner receives the individual check. Use a fresh ruler measurement and change one delay during the exit checks. Compared with the source procedure, look for sounder scale-based choices while tracking the displaced cost: less group calculation time and greater reliance on teacher-supplied distances. Stop repeated remeasurement at the two-minute boundary. If learners can compare provided times but cannot explain scale, record that outcome as unmet; the recovery rule has not repaired their understanding. No improvement is established before this trial.

EXPAND.title: Turn unit labels into supported conversion decisions
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: “Build a units gate between distance and time.” Preserve its mechanism: distinguish what each number measures and what additional information permits the next conversion. Its consequential gap is that peers ask learners to justify conversions but have no everyday response when an explanation fails. Add a short teacher-owned recovery routine during practice.

Use two maps at tables of six, rulers, pencils, supplied example speeds and the classroom clock. The teacher first checks a readable scale, connected candidate paths and manageable calculations. Measure along mapped paths; neither a straight line nor a printed connection establishes a safe or accessible walking route.

Minutes 0–6: demonstrate centimetres on map → metres along route → estimated minutes. Explain both conversions and model uncertainty about speed and delays. Minutes 6–15: rotate measuring, converting and explaining. A peer asks what the number measures and what supports the conversion. If the learner cannot explain after one prompt, the peer stops approving further conversions and alerts the teacher. Within one minute, the teacher points to the relevant scale or supplied speed, models one conversion, and asks the learner to explain a different simple example. If arithmetic remains the obstacle, provide the result and assess its meaning. If the conceptual explanation still fails, retain the worked example for supported practice and flag that criterion for the individual check. Do not let a group queue form: unresolved cases return to supported practice while the teacher moves on.

Minutes 15–23: compare a second candidate route, explicitly introducing hypothetical delays where needed. Ask learners to make a conditional choice and explain which missing information could change it. A missing speed prevents a numerical moving-time estimate; missing access information limits a route recommendation. It does not erase the measured distance.

Minutes 23–35: twelve one-minute individual checks, each covering scale, route choice using distance and time, and uncertainty with an effect. Accept pointing and oral answers, read labels aloud, and separate arithmetic difficulty from conceptual misunderstanding. Record all three criteria in a map margin.

This adds brief targeted instruction rather than more unit questions. It assumes teacher access to both groups and readable map scales; it cannot remedy inaccessible print or verify street conditions.
EXPAND.experiment: The teacher trials the procedure once, comparing its practical value with the source’s peer questioning alone. Record how many failed explanations receive a recovery attempt, whether learners subsequently explain a fresh conversion, and whether intervention time crowds out route comparison. Include an exit prompt giving distance without speed, followed by a supplied speed, so learners must both identify the missing input and proceed once it is available. Stop individual interventions at one minute and use the supported example fallback. Retain the change only if individual scale, route-choice and uncertainty explanations benefit without losing the twelve-person check. Reciting unit labels alone does not count as understanding.

EXPAND.title: Have learners construct a counterexample to their own planning rule
EXPAND.proposal:
New mechanism: learners generate a counterexample to an overgeneralized rule, then replace it with a conditional rule. Producing two possible journeys with the same route distance but different travel times makes distance alone insufficient by construction. This removes the need to begin with two distinct measurable routes or a teacher-planted faulty recommendation.

The teacher owns the lesson. Use the two printed maps, rulers, pencils, example walking speeds and classroom clock. Preparation requires one readable scale and one traceable path per group; the teacher checks its distance and a manageable time calculation. Hypothetical speeds or delays describe teaching scenarios, not neighborhood facts. Printed connections and straight lines establish neither safe crossings nor accessibility.

Minutes 0–6: model scale and measure a short route along its segments. Explain how distance and assumed speed produce moving time. Minutes 6–10: each learner states a provisional rule for choosing or timing a walking route, orally if preferred. The teacher then sets the construction challenge: keep endpoints and route distance fixed, but create two plausible hypothetical journeys with different travel times using the supplied speeds or an explicitly invented waiting delay.

Minutes 10–18: at two tables of six, learners work in pairs, sharing the map. Each pair measures or checks part of the route and constructs its two journeys. Each learner explains which input changed and why distance stayed fixed. If a pair cannot construct an example after two minutes, the teacher supplies one delay and asks them to complete and explain it; they then change the delay themselves.

Minutes 18–23: pairs replace their initial rule with a conditional planning rule: measure a candidate path using scale, estimate time from speed and delays, and make route choice conditional on relevant missing information. If a second mapped path is available, apply the rule to it; otherwise explain why the current information supports only a provisional choice of the measured path.

Minutes 23–35: twelve individual one-minute checks. Each learner interprets scale, explains a route choice using time assumptions, and identifies an uncertainty and its effect. Include a brief same-distance example to check the central distinction. Permit pointing, oral answers, teacher-read labels and arithmetic support.

The approach may reveal reasoning more directly than following worked comparisons, but generating examples adds cognitive demand. Its fallback is a partly completed example, and its limits include shared-map access and unverified real-world conditions.
EXPAND.experiment: The teacher runs one bounded trial. During construction, inspect whether learners genuinely hold distance fixed while changing a time input. At exit, use an unfamiliar delay or speed and ask for an explanation, alongside the required scale and route-choice checks. Compare with a teacher-led route comparison: assess independent explanations and record the extra prompting and time needed to generate examples. Stop open-ended construction after two unsuccessful minutes per pair and provide the partial example. If learners only repeat that 'anything could happen,' cannot explain the changed input, or lose scale understanding, the generative mechanism has not earned its extra burden. No superiority is assumed.
